title: Habits (ST I-II.49–54)
hookLine: we become what we repeatedly do

lines: A DIRT PATH ACROSS THE LAWN.
HOW DOES A PERSON GET ANYWHERE?
cards: At the corner of a park there's a strip of dirt cutting diagonally across the lawn. Nobody planned it. No crew laid it.
It's there because people kept taking the shortcut, one pair of shoes at a time, until the grass gave up. Now it's the path, and new walkers take it without thinking.

After yesterday's far horizon, Thomas comes down to the ground under our feet: how does a person actually get anywhere? His answer is today's word, habitus. Or, as an old saying puts it, we become what we repeatedly do.

teach.h: HABITUS: SOMETHING YOU COME TO HAVE.
teach.b: Thomas himself links habitus to habere, to have. A habit is something you come to have, a settled readiness to act. It isn't a single action.
It's what's left in you after many actions: the worn path in the grass.

teach.h: OUR POWERS CAN GO MANY WAYS.
teach.b: We need habits, Thomas says, because our powers can go many ways. An eye just sees. But a will can lean toward patience or toward snapping, toward truth or the easy lie.
Habits tilt those powers one way, so the next choice comes more easily.

teach.h: ACTS MAKE HABITS; HABITS CAN FADE.
teach.b: And acts make them. Each act leaves a trace; repeat it and the trace deepens.

A good habit of this kind is what the tradition calls a virtue; a bad one, a vice. That's the sobering half. The hopeful half: habits can weaken and fade, by not acting on them, or by acting against them.
The path grows back if people stop walking it. On Thomas's account, no one has to stay the person their worst habit made.

teach.h: BY CUSTOM HAVE THEIR SENSES EXERCISED.
teach.b: The Letter to the Hebrews, in the Douay-Rheims, says the perfect are those "who by custom have their senses exercised to the discerning of good and evil." By custom. Exercised.
Discernment, too, is a path walked many times. So when the Church talks about holiness, it isn't only talking about big conversions.
It's the ordinary repeated act, the kindness done on a tired Wednesday, that makes the next one a little easier.

how: Catholic moral teaching describes the virtues as good habits strengthened by repeated acts, and spiritual directors often suggest one small daily practice, such as an examen at night or grace at meals, to build them.

o: a settled readiness built by repeated acts
a single choice that changes your life
a passing urge that comes and goes

s: for Thomas, a habit is a single action
it's what's left in you after many actions: a settled readiness to act.
Thomas says habits can weaken by not acting on them
habits fade through disuse or contrary acts, like a path that grows back.
Thomas thinks we need habits because our powers can only go one way
it's the opposite: powers like the will can go many ways, so habits tilt them.

games.q: you're a student of Thomas with a bad habit of snapping at people. what does his teaching on habits say about it?
o: it can weaken by not acting on it and by acting against it.
it doesn't matter: habits don't affect choices.
games.why: Thomas says habits are made by acts and can fade through disuse or contrary acts. the path grows back.

practice: Think of one small good you'd like to come easier a month from now: saying thank you out loud, a pause before replying, a short prayer at a meal, the phone in another room at night.
Keep it tiny, then picture its first step in the place it would actually happen, the kitchen, the car, the bedside, and walk it once in your mind: the first footprint on the path.
If you pray, offer the habit to God before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Habitus. For Thomas, a settled readiness to act that grows from repeated acts. A good one is a virtue, a bad one a vice. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: a settled disposition, something a person has come to have.

carryVoice: Your line: we become our habits. One footprint starts a path. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.q: who by custom have their senses exercised to the discerning of good and evil.
